correctness.rationale: Let \(X=V(G)\setminus D\), \(q=|X|\), and \(t=q-k\). For a selected vertex in part \(V_i\), the number of outside neighbors is exactly \(q-x_i\); the capacity condition is therefore \(x_i\ge t\), equivalently \(d_i\le n_i-t\). A minimum solution has \(q\ge k\), cannot be a singleton in the range \(k<\Delta(G)\), and when \(t>0\) cannot lie in a single part, giving the stated bounds on \(t\). Summing the part capacities yields \(\sum_i\min(n_i,t)\le k+t\). Conversely, any feasible \(t\) provides at least two positive part capacities whose total is at least \(N-k-t\), so one can choose a dominating set meeting two parts and satisfying every capacity inequality. The balanced specialization reduces exactly to \((r-1)t\le k\).
risks: The theorem is only for the stated nontrivial range \(1\le k<\Delta(G)\); the finite order-11 verifier is corroborative and not used as the universal proof.

value.rationale: Complete multipartite graphs are a standard structural family containing cliques, stars, bicliques, and Turán graphs. The theorem strictly extends the initiating paper's exact biclique result, gives a sharp one-dimensional criterion for every part profile, and yields a closed balanced formula. This is a motivated complete family classification rather than an arbitrary slice.
